principles.principle: Move the argument forward by contrast: adversative connectives (However, Yet, an alternative view) set one position against another, and concessive constructions (While X, we nonetheless Y) grant a point before overturning or qualifying it.
principles.why: Staging competing views as a tension the paper will resolve creates forward momentum and makes the contribution feel earned rather than asserted; the reader is pulled through claim and counter-claim.

principles.principle: The intro opens not on the specific result but on the broad subject, asserting its importance or centrality in a sweeping, confident declarative opening — often in elevated or attention-getting diction (small-caps lead-ins, 'plays a central role', 'a growing body', 'in this day and age'). The first sentence stakes out wide territory before any narrowing to the paper's own question.
principles.why: Starting wide gives an unprimed reader a frame to hang everything else on, and the slightly grand, stakes-asserting register earns attention and signals that the topic matters before the technical narrowing begins.

principles.principle: The intro discloses the findings rather than holding them back for suspense, typically via a flagged 'we find / our results show' clause carrying concrete directional or numeric detail.
principles.why: Front-loading the answer lets the reader process the rest of the paper as confirmation and extract the contribution at low cost, while the concrete specifics signal the claims are already empirically realized rather than merely promised.

principles.principle: Open the intro by asserting the topic's broad importance, then in the same breath pivot to what prior work has ignored, left unexplained, or barely studied, framing the paper as filling a named void.
principles.why: Establishing the stakes earns the reader's attention, and naming the gap immediately gives the paper an instant reason to exist, so within a few sentences the reader knows why the work is needed.

principles.principle: Speak in an active first-person authorial voice that openly narrates what the paper does and what it finds, using constructions like 'In this paper, we show/propose...' and 'I find that...'.
principles.why: The direct we-do/we-find voice keeps agency visible and the prose concrete and brisk, so the reader always knows who is doing what and can follow the paper's actions and results without decoding passive abstractions.

principles.principle: Dense material is broken into explicitly counted, grammatically parallel slots — 'First… Second… Third…', '(1)… (2)…', 'contributes in two ways', 'makes three contributions', 'adds to the literature in several ways'. The number is announced up front and each item opens with a matching ordinal in parallel syntax.
principles.why: Pre-announcing the count and marching through parallel items lets the reader keep a running tally and chunk otherwise tangled claims into a clean list, lowering the effort of holding a multi-part argument in mind.

principles.principle: Each intro carries an explicit, self-aware contribution statement built from a small recurring vocabulary ('novel', 'contribution(s)', 'we contribute / our study adds') that names what is new and pins it against prior work.
principles.why: An overt contribution clause hands editors and readers the paper's novelty claim directly instead of forcing them to infer it, which is the central currency the genre trades in.

principles.principle: The introduction closes with a dedicated signpost paragraph that maps the paper section by section in a near-fixed formula — 'The remainder of the paper is organized/proceeds as follows. Section 2 …, Section 3 …' — each clause pairing a section number with a verb naming what that section does.
principles.why: Ending on an explicit prose table of contents hands the reader a navigation key and sets expectations for the route ahead, so the body that follows never feels disorienting.

evidence.quote: The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 reviews the relevant prior literature.

principles.principle: Ground an abstract construct in a concrete particular or a borrowed authoritative voice, an epigraph, a named real-world episode, or a quotation from a dictionary, philosopher, or prior scholar.
principles.why: A vivid particular or quoted authority makes an otherwise dry, abstract construct tangible and memorable, hooking the reader and lending the framing outside credibility.

redteam_rejected.reason: Conflates two distinct devices under one over-broad 'explicit signposting' label: in-text ordinal enumeration (First/Second within the argument) and the terminal section-by-section roadmap ('The remainder of the paper... Section 2...'). These are separable stylistic moves serving different functions in different places, and both are retained separately here — enumeration as the canonical a2-p4 and the roadmap as the canonical a2-p5. As a single bundled principle it is redundant and too coarse to act on.

side_notes: Coverage gap: all 18 principles operate at the discourse/rhetorical-move level (broad openings, gap-pivots, contrast, signposting/enumeration, contribution claims, section roadmaps, first-person voice, concrete anchors, results-up-front). No agent examined sentence- or micro-level style — sentence length and rhythm, hedging vs. assertive certainty, active/passive balance, paragraph length, or citation-integration mechanics (e.g., the parenthetical bracketed cite form '(Kothari, Shu, and Wysocki [2009])'). A human may want this layer probed.

Coverage gap: a rhetorical-question opener appears in the verified evidence (bertrand_schoar2003 para 0: 'How much do individual managers matter for firm behavior and economic performance?') but none of the three agents isolates 'open the intro by posing the research question directly' as its own device.

Synthesis note for the human: the kept opening trio is intentionally granular and lightly overlapping — a2-p1 (broad importance/elevated-diction overture, with standalone pure-opener evidence in lm2011/dwz/ragozzino), a1-p1 (the importance->gap funnel pivot), and a1-p2 (adversative/concessive contrast as a general argument engine: 'However...costs', 'An alternative view', 'While X, we Y'). They are kept distinct because each has independent evidence and a different rhetorical function (opener register vs. gap-naming pivot vs. competing-view staging), but a reviewer may judge a2-p1 and a1-p1 close enough to fold.
